title: BARRINGTON, George. A VOYAGE TO NEW SOUTH WALES; With a Description of the Country; The Manners, Customs, Religion, &c.
description: BARRINGTON, George. A VOYAGE TO NEW SOUTH WALES; With a Description of the Country; The Manners, Customs, Religion, &c. of the Natives, in the Vicinity of Botany Bay. Octavo, soiled endpapers, contemporary speckled calf, boxed. London, Printed for the Proprietor; Sold by H. D. Symonds, 1795. The rare first edition of the original ‘Barrington’ voyage account, published by a prominent London publisher of chapbooks and other cheaper books. Much news was coming back to England by various sources which added to the information provided by Hunter and Tench in 1793, but no new books had been published to satisfy the public demand that clearly still existed, particularly among the less well-to-do who could not afford the expensive journals of the First Fleet officers. Accordingly, Symonds used this scattered and often ephemeral material to compile this account of the voyage to Botany Bay and of eighteenth-century New South Wales which he published under Barrington’s profitable name. Consequently, the ‘Barrington’ account includes many details of the colony not elsewhere available and, perhaps more importantly, this text in its numerous versions became the predominant source of information about the settlement for the greater part of the British public. Reprinted and pirated dozens of times, the ‘Barrington’ account of New South Wales was, with Mary Ann Parker’s Voyage, one of only two books to describe the voyage of the Third Fleet and the state of the settlement on its arrival late in 1791 when the colony was starved of supplies. It was sufficiently well regarded for a French translation to have been published as well as several American editions. Ferguson, 205; Garvey, AB1; Wantrup, 25. Estimate $3000/5000 Illustrated online at Invaluable.com

In November 1766 Bougainville set sail from Nantes for South America, setting off from Chile he sailed directly across the Pacific, taking possession of the Tuamotu Archipelago. He also mistakenly took possession of Tahiti, not realising that Wallis had already discovered it shortly before. Nevertheless, Bougainville’s detailed account of the island and its people aroused great interest in Europe, where it became a significant source for the romantic vision of the South Pacific. After a long stay in Tahiti he visited Samoa and the New Hebrides. From there, he planned to sail directly west to clear up the mystery of the east coast of New Holland. title: BROSSES, Charles de. HISTOIRE DES NAVIGATIONS AUX TERRES AUSTRALES Contenant ce que l’on sçait des moeurs & des producti
description: BROSSES, Charles de. HISTOIRE DES NAVIGATIONS AUX TERRES AUSTRALES Contenant ce que l’on sçait des moeurs & des productions des Contrées découvertes jusqu’à ce jour; & où il est traité de l’utilité d’y faire de plus amples découvertes, & des moyens d’y former un établissement. Two volumes, quarto, seven folding engraved maps (one with pale marks), with the additional asterisked leaves in volume one, scattered toning and foxing, contemporary cat’s paw calf, spine with raised bands and gilt in compartments, one hinge neatly refurbished, double contrasting labels. Paris, Durand, 1756. First edition: “One of the outstanding works relating to the early history of Australasia” (Hill), and one of the most influential works dealing with early voyages to the Pacific. De Brosses’s two volumes played a fundamental role in the growing imperative in both Britain and France for greater engagement with the new lands discovered over the preceding century. De Brosses took care to include accounts of all southern voyages, from the Vespucci voyage of 1502 up to the end of the 1740s, including among others the voyages of Magellan, Drake, Quirós, Le Maire, and Tasman. The maps include those of Australia (“Carte réduite de l’Australie pour servir à la lecture de l’Histoire des Terres Australes…”, by Robert de Vaugondy), New Guinea, and north-eastern Australia. De Brosses, who profoundly influenced Bougainville, sought to encourage French discovery in the South Seas and also argued for programmatic colonisation. As a judge, he was acutely aware of the difficulties facing the poor in France and his proposals for settling the southern hemisphere are based on his concern for improving their condition. It is ironic that his proposals for colonisation were used ten years later, without acknowledgement, by John Callander as the basis for his influential Terra Australis Cognita. Captain James Cook had a copy of De Brosses with him on the Endeavour voyage. description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King... [together with] AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement, in January 1788, to August 1801: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King; and an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr Bass... Vol. II. Two volumes, quarto, containing in total three maps, 23 plates (three coloured) and eight half-page engravings (two coloured), some general offsetting and toning as usual, small erasure from second title-page, ink blots on a couple of leaves, paper flaw in second List of Engravings, occasional fingermarks, the final gatherings of second volume water-stained, in handsome recent half calf and marbled boards, corners vellum-tipped. London, Printed by A. Strahan for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798 – 1802. First and best edition. Written by Judge Advocate David Collins, this was the last of the First Fleet journals and the most detailed accounts of the voyage and first settlement. The second volume, based almost entirely on the papers of Governor Hunter supplemented by official records and dispatches, is significantly more uncommon than the first volume. It is of great importance, both for its chronicle of later events and for the narratives of voyages and expeditions of discovery undertaken in the intervening years. These include the first printing of Flinders’s log of his northern voyage of 1799 in the Norfolk along the Queensland coast, as well as the inland expeditions of John Price and Henry Hacking that include the first report of the existence of the koala, the earliest recorded sighting of a wombat on mainland Australia and the first report of the discovery of the lyre-bird, which is here described and illustrated in colour for the first time. In particular, this second volume is of high Victorian interest. Through his friend and collaborator, Governor John Hunter, Collins had access to the journal of George Bass. This he reproduces in detail, a fact that is noted on the title-page of the second volume stating that it included “an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr. Bass”. This was the only publication of Bass’s journal of the discovery of the strait that bears his name. Ferguson, 263 and 350; Wantrup, 19 and 20. description: DUMONT D’URVILLE, Jules Sébastien César. VOYAGE DE LA CORVETTE L’ASTROLABE exécuté par Ordre du Roi, pendant les années 1826 – 1827 – 1828 – 1829, sous le commandement de M. J. The scientific voyage of the Astrolabe was arguably the most important and the most influential nineteenth-century French voyage to the Pacific. In addition to its comprehensive hydrographical work, especially in New Zealand, the Astrolabe scientists made extensive observations and vast collections of natural history specimens. The outstanding results of the expedition were published in thirteen text volumes and five large atlases from 1830 to 1835. These atlases contain what are generally acknowledged to be some of the finest plates ever produced of the natural history, topography, and anthropology of the Australia and the South-west Pacific. Most of the fine topographical views are after Louis Auguste de Sainson. The official account of the voyage is rarely found complete. title: GRANT, James. THE NARRATIVE OF A VOYAGE OF DISCOVERY, performed in His Majesty’s Vessel The Lady Nelson... in the years
description: GRANT, James. THE NARRATIVE OF A VOYAGE OF DISCOVERY, performed in His Majesty’s Vessel The Lady Nelson... in the years 1800, 1801 and 1802, to New South Wales... Quarto, with large folding plate of sliding keels, folding chart (offset), six plates (one handcoloured), with the rare blank leaf d4, one opening with small text loss through adhesion, contemporary half calf and marbled boards, spine chipped and front joint showing a split at foot, corners rubbed, with the engraved armorial bookplate of Joseph Cotton. London, Printed by C. Rowarth for T. Egerton, 1803. First edition. The discovery of the Victorian coast; a foundation item for Victoria. In 1800 James Grant was instructed to sail the Lady Nelson from England to Sydney where it was intended he would hand her over to Matthew Flinders. In the course of the voyage, Grant was instructed him to search for the western passage into Bass Strait and traverse it from west to east. This he succeeded in doing, making landfall on what is now the Victorian coast near Mt Schank and Mt Gambier, discovering the Victorian coastline west of Bass’s discoveries of 1797 and 1798. He named most of the features on the coast he discovered. On 8 December he discovered a bay which he named Governor King’s Bay. He was unable to enter it and could not know what a momentous discovery he almost made: it is now known as Port Phillip Bay. When Grant reached Sydney, Governor King sent him to chart the entire south-east coast. Bad weather, however, made this impossible and only part of Bass Strait was surveyed, from Western Port to Wilson’s Promontory. Later in 1801 Grant and Lieutenant-Governor William Paterson explored the Hunter River in the Lady Nelson, which led to the establishment of the future city of Newcastle. Grant’s Narrative is a very scarce book, especially in contemporary binding. “It is of the highest significance to any collection of Australian books and no collection of books dealing with coastal discovery or with Victoria can be without it” (Wantrup). Clancy, 9.4; Davidson, pp. 125-6 (“a rare and most desirable item”); Ferguson, 375 (not noting the blank leaf d4); Hill 2, 718; Wantrup, 75. title: GREY, George. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS OF DISCOVERY in North-West and Western Australia, during the years 1837, 38, a
description: GREY, George. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS OF DISCOVERY in North-West and Western Australia, during the years 1837, 38, and 39, Under the Authority of Her Majesty’s Government. title: [IMAGINARY VOYAGE] KILLIGREW, Thomas, The Younger, or Charles GILDON (attributed).
description: [IMAGINARY VOYAGE] KILLIGREW, Thomas, The Younger, or Charles GILDON (attributed). MISCELLANEA AUREA: OR THE GOLDEN MEDLEY. Consisting of I. A Voyage to the Mountains of the Moon… II. The Fortunate Shipwreck, or a Description of New Athens, being an Account of the Laws, Manners, Religion, and Customs of that Country; by Morris Williams, Gent. who resided there above Twenty Years… Octavo, one short tear repaired, more recent antique-style half calf and marbled boards. London, Bettesworth and Pemberton, 1720. Rare: first edition of this literary miscellany. The second piece in the volume, “The Fortunate Shipwreck, or a Description of New Athens, being an Account of the Laws, Manners, Religion, and Customs of that Country” is an often overlooked Australian fictitious voyage. New Athens is an utopian outpost, settled hundreds of years before by a huge expedition of Greeks escaping turmoil in their homeland. After a three-year voyage, they reach Terra Australis Incognita where they intermarry with the “Aborigines” – is this the first use of the term in an Australian context? – and present their visitor, Morris Williams, Gent., with “one of the happiest cities in the world, for peace tranquillity, and health are ensured by the absence of lawyers, apothecaries, and the needy poor...” (Gibson). The newcomers, however, soon teach the New Athenians how to manufacture gunpowder! Published anonymously the year after Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe, parts of the work are attributed to Thomas Killigrew and others to Charles Gildon, although recent scholarship concludes that the imaginary voyage, “New Athens”, was written mainly, if not entirely, by Killigrew (1657-1719). title: [IMAGINARY VOYAGE: TYSSOT DE PATOT, Simon].
description: [IMAGINARY VOYAGE: TYSSOT DE PATOT, Simon]. VOYAGES ET AVANTURES DE JAQUES MASSÉ. Duodecimo, contemporary mottled calf, spine fully gilt, marbled endpapers, engraved bookplate. Bordeaux, Jacques l’Aveugle, 1710 [i.e. The Hague?, T. Johnson?, circa 1714-1717]. The true first edition of this celebrated imaginary voyage, published in The Hague circa 1714-7 with a false imprint dated 1710. Huguenot freethinker Tyssot de Patot’s account of the voyage of Jacques Massé is as much a work of libertine philosophy as an imaginary or utopian voyage. Massé, a French surgeon, is shipwrecked on an island in the South Sea – near to where Kerguelen Island is in fact situated – with 85 survivors. He describes how they set about establishing an encampment and building a raft, giving also a circumstantial account of the island and its natural productions. When exploring the interior he and a companion encounter an advanced civilisation – monarchical, deistic and utopian – in a land of plenty. The dangerously freethinking, anti-clerical nature of much of the discussion that takes place between the hero and his hosts partly explains the false imprints on the several early editions of this book, which continued to be read, reprinted, and translated well into the century. title: JUKES, Joseph Beete. NARRATIVE OF THE SURVEYING VOYAGE OF H.M.S. FLY, Commanded by Captain F.P. Blackwood, R.N. in Torre

Attached to the expedition were the marine geologist Joseph Beete Jukes, the zoologist John Macgillivray, and the artist Harden Melville. From 1842 to 1846 they made a careful survey of the coast between Sandy Cape and Torres Strait, and explored the southern coasts of New Guinea, discovering most notably the Fly River. title: [KERGUELEN-TRÉMAREC] PAGÈS, Pierre Marie François, Vicomte de.
description: [KERGUELEN-TRÉMAREC] PAGÈS, Pierre Marie François, Vicomte de. VOYAGES AUTOUR DU MONDE, ET VERS LES DEUX POLES. Par Terre et par Mer, Pendant les Années 1767, 1768, 1769, 1770, 1771, 1773, 1774 & 1776... Two volumes, octavo, ten folding engraved maps and plates, a fine crisp copy, contemporary mottled calf, marbled endpapers. Paris, Moutard, 1782. A fine set of the rare first edition: Pagès account of his travels including the disastrous second expedition of Yves-Joseph Kerguelen-Trémarec. Pagès, a French naval officer, travelled extensively throughout North America, Asia, and the Middle East in 1767-1771. After returning to France, he joined the second expedition of the aristocratic naval officer, Yves-Joseph Kerguelen-Trémarec, in 1773-1774. This abortive expedition, an official French voyage towards the South Pole in search of the supposed Gonneville Land and the French court’s answer to the voyages of James Cook, was a complete disaster, almost entirely due to the venal, incompetent, and cowardly aristocrat who was given charge of it. The Pagès account of the expedition is effectively the only accessible one since Kerguelen’s published account was rigorously suppressed after his court-martial. Kerguelen was dismissed from the navy and imprisoned. His contribution to discovery was negligible. Apart from the rather insignificant discovery of Kerguelen Island in his first voyage, the results of which he deliberately exaggerated so as to gain command of a second expedition, he achieved nothing despite the thousands of livres the government spent on his expeditions. However, “it was he who finally persuaded the French that Terra Australis was a fiction – something which Cook was demonstrating to the world in general, but which the French, so influenced by the Gonneville tradition, needed to have emphasized” (Dunmore). The plates include a map of his route on an earlier trip from New Orleans up the Mississippi, then by canoe on the Red River to Nachitoches, and overland through San Antonio and Mexico City to Acapulco. Hill 2, 1285 (English edition); Renard, 1186 (English edition); not in Rosove; Sabin, 58168; Spence 2, 887; see also Dunmore, I, pp. 196 – 249. title: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY OF THE INTERTROPICAL AND WESTERN COASTS OF AUSTRALIA. Performed between the
description: KING, Phillip Parker. NARRATIVE OF A SURVEY OF THE INTERTROPICAL AND WESTERN COASTS OF AUSTRALIA. Performed between the years 1818 and 1822... With an appendix, containing various subjects relating to Hydrography and Natural History. In two volumes, illustrated by plates, charts, and wood-cuts. Two volumes, octavo, plates and maps, folding map, the plates and maps a little offset and foxed as usual, errata leaf for both volumes in volume two (as issued), bound without half-titles in contemporary polished calf, marbled edges and endpapers, top of the spines a little worn, the copy of Sir Charles Edward Stirling with armorial bookplate, in modern folding book box with the bookplate of Geoffrey Cains. London, John Murray, 1826. First edition: the extremely rare first issue with title-pages dated 1826. Admiral Phillip Parker King, Australian-born son of the third governor, Philip Gidley King, became the Navy’s leading hydrographer. Despatched by the Admiralty and the Colonial Office to complete Flinders’s interrupted survey and firmly to establish Great Britain’s claim to the north coast, King charted the greater part of the west, north and north-east coasts and also carried out important surveys in the area of the Barrier Reef. His coastal voyages and Oxley’s expeditions inland were the great expansionary undertakings of the Macquarie era. His hydrographical work is still the basis of many of the modern charts for the areas he surveyed. First published in April 1826, the first issue of this classic Australian voyage is “a notorious rarity” (Wantrup). Late in 1826 or early in 1827 the publisher, John Murray, had the original title-page dated 1826 excised and replaced with a cancel title-page dated 1827. Known to Ferguson in only one copy and to Davidson in less than a handful, about a dozen are now recorded. It is one of the most conspicuous rarities in Australian collecting. title: LEICHHARDT, Friedrich Wilhelm Ludwig.
description: LEICHHARDT, Friedrich Wilhelm Ludwig. JOURNAL OF AN OVERLAND EXPEDITION IN AUSTRALIA, from Moreton Bay to Port Essington, a distance of upwards of 3000 miles, during the years 1844 – 1845. Two volumes, octavo, text with frontispiece and six aquatint plates (one folding) in the original dark olive green cloth of the primary issue (varnished), together with the separately-issued three-sheet map in a sympathetic modern cloth case of matching colour, maps with pale offsetting and some splits at folds, the first sheet of the map with several ink spots. London, T. & W. Boone, 1847. With the rare three-sheet map. First edition: one of the most important works of Australian inland exploration. In the course of this harrowing journey, Leichhardt and his party explored over three thousand miles of completely unknown country in fourteen months, opening up a vast and valuable area of the interior. Despite poor bushcraft and constant harassment from Aborigines, Leichhardt’s meandering journey from Brisbane to Port Essington ranks among Australia’s most successful expeditions. His scientific and geographic work were greatly admired during his lifetime and, after he vanished on a later expedition, his unknown fate became part of the mythology of European Australia. The separately-issued three-sheet map is one of the great rarities of Australian exploration literature. Abbey, 579 (text only); Ferguson, 4571 (text only); Richards, 101; Wantrup, 138a (text) and 139 (map). + LEICHHARDT’S SIGNATURE in BAILEY, N. THE UNIVERSAL ETYMOLOGICAL ENGLISH DICTIONARY, Second edition, with many additions. Thick octavo, half calf and marbled boards, housed in modern cloth book box. London, Thomas Cox at the Lamb under the Royal-Exchange, 1731. Signed, on a rear blank, in his hand by Ludwig Leichhardt: a book that was doubtless in daily use during the preparation for publication of the explorer’s own Journal. Such relics of the explorers, especially Leichhardt, are extremely rare on the market. Estimate $18,000/20,000 Illustrated online at Invaluable.com

title: LISIANSKY, Captain Urey.
description: LISIANSKY, Captain Urey. A VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD, in the years 1803, 4, 5, & 6; Performed by order of His Imperial Majesty Alexander the First, Emperor of Russia, in the ship Neva. Quarto, engraved portrait frontispiece, eight hand coloured Arrowsmith maps (3 folding), one (of two) hand coloured aquatint views (lacking the Harbour of St. Paul), 3 engraved plates, one Contents leaf bound out of order in the Appendix, the text with some professional paper paper repairs (small loss in two cases) and sealed tears, some general browning and foxing, several erased stamps, recent diced calf in period style, boards with elaborate gilt border, outer and lower edges uncut, marbled endpapers. Lisiansky parted from Krusenstern in the Marquesas, and spent ten days in Hawaii before heading to Alaska and Kamchatka for fur trading and the re-supply of trading posts and missions. After spending the summer of 1805 in Sitka he left for Canton. The attractive maps and plates are from Lisiansky’s own surveys and drawings. See Abbey Travel 4; Forbes 443; Sabin 41416. title: [MAGRA, James]. SUPPLÉMENT AU VOYAGE DE M. DE BOUGAINVILLE, ou Journal d’un Voyage Autour du Monde, Fait par MM. Banks &
description: [MAGRA, James]. SUPPLÉMENT AU VOYAGE DE M. DE BOUGAINVILLE, ou Journal d’un Voyage Autour du Monde, Fait par MM. Banks & Solander, Anglois, en 1768, 1769, 1770, 1771. Traduit de l’Anglois, par M. de Fréville. Octavo, one preliminary leaf remargined, bound with the half-title in contemporary patterned calf, expertly rebacked. Paris, Saillant & Nyon, 1772. The first French edition of James Magra’s surreptitious account of Cook’s first voyage that had been published anonymously in 1771 by Becket and de Hondt several years before the publication of Hawkesworth’s official account. As du Rietz pointed out (Kroepelien, 218), “the French, before the appearance of Hawkesworth’s work in 1773, believed the anonymous account of 1771 to be the official narrative of the expedition, the announced forthcoming work by Hawkesworth being supposed to deal with the scientific observations only”. Notice also that the voyage is credited to Banks and Solander, with Cook, a mere nautical servant, not even noticed. This issue was published as a supplementary volume to the 1772 Paris octavo edition of Bougainville’s Voyage Autour du Monde – there is some irony in that, since Cook achieved what Bougainville set out to do. Despite this – or perhaps because of this – Cook’s successful voyage is relegated to being a ‘supplement’ to the account of Bougainville’s non-achievement. Beddie, 697; Kroepelien, 219. title: MALASPINA. VIANA, Francisco Xavier de.
description: MALASPINA. VIANA, Francisco Xavier de. DIARIO DEL VIAGE EXPLORADOR de las Corbetas Espanolas “Descubierta” y “Atrevida” en los anos de 1789 a 1794. Octavo, with one of the two title-pages, with a typographical frame to each page, a couple of gatherings browned, some margins with the page numbers lost or trimmed by the binder, LACKING the two final leaves of tables (supplied in facsimile), with the loosely inserted bookplate of Jorge Skinner-Klee, contemporary vellum with later spine label, housed in quarter morocco book box. [Montevideo], Cerrito de la Victoria, Imprenta del Ejercito, 1849. Earliest account of the Malaspina expedition at Port Jackson 1793. Only edition of one of the rarest Pacific voyages, the great scientific expedition under Alessandro Malaspina, 1789 to 1794, throughout the Pacific, exploring and mapping much of the west coast of the Americas from Cape Horn to the Gulf of Alaska, then across to the Philippines, with stops in Australia and New Zealand. While the Malaspina expedition was planned as the Spanish answer to Cook and La Pérouse, the ill-advised involvement of the commander in a court intrigue once back in Madrid led to his imprisonment and the complete suppression of the planned official account, including the scientific and other results. The earliest account of the voyage was published in 1849 by Francisco Xavier de Viana, who had served as an ensign on the expedition and later settled in Uraguay, where this rare account was printed. Lada-Mocarski considered that “[Viana’s] diary is of immense value. It is the only full and detailed printed account of Malaspina’s voyage from California to Alaska by one of the participants”. It is also of considerable Australian importance. The Spanish visit to Port Jackson came only five years after the foundation of the colony and caused considerable interest in Sydney, Collins, for example, gives an extended account of their visit. One expedition member wrote to Sir Joseph Banks of “the very extraordinary humanity and kindness with which the English in their new Colony welcomed us” and while there the scientists made good use of their time. The artists also made a very fine series of drawings at Port Jackson, a valuable record of the state of the colony and including the only known depictions of convicts at that period. Viana’s extended account of Sydney at this crucial time is one of very few published (and unpublished) accounts of the infant colony by an independent eye-witness. His book is rare, perhaps, as Lada-Mocarski speculates: “For some reason Viana’s diary was published on the travelling press of the Army besieging Montevideo, during the war between Argentina and Uruguay. This is the reason for the extreme rarity of this important diary…”. Ferguson, 5100 (and 5228, very confused by the two title-pages); not in Hill; Lada-Mocarski, 134; not in Sabin; not in Wagner. See further A. Grove Day and Virginia M. Day, The Spanish at Port Jackson (Sydney, Australian Documentary Facsimile Society 1967), which includes a facsimile and a translation of the Port Jackson section. Second edition, printed in the same year as the first: the great scientific expedition under Alessandro Malaspina, 1789 to 1794, throughout the Pacific, exploring and mapping much of the west coast of the Americas from Cape Horn to the Gulf of Alaska, then across to the Philippines, with stops in Australia and New Zealand. title: [MELVILLE] BOONE, Thomas.
description: [MELVILLE] BOONE, Thomas. AUTOGRAPH LETTER, SIGNED, TO I.B. DAVIS, ESQ. One page one one leaf, octavo, ink manuscript; fine. [London, circa 1849] An important letter from publisher Thomas Boone to the recipient who had evidently sought information about Harden S. Melville’s volume of illustrations to the Fly voyage, which Boone had promoted briefly in 1849. “The firm’s prudent reliance on subscription is underlined by their dealings with Harden Melville, whose A Series of Twenty-five Drawings selected from a folio of Sketches taken in Australia and the Adjacent Islands was the subject of a single-leaf advertisement found only in the first issue of Charles Sturt’s Narrative of an Expedition into Central Australia (it is a key marker of the first issue). The advertisement sought subscribers to the twenty-five-plate work at one guinea. The advertisement was quickly discontinued and Boone did not undertake the publication. The firm’s approach to publishing was by no means sentimental: in an undated letter Thomas Boone wrote, somewhat disingenuously, in response to an enquiry about Melville’s work that “I believe a publication of Views in Australia was at one time contemplated by Mr Melville … but certainly no Separate Work ever appeared – I doubt if a Publisher would be willing to risk the cost, & presume sufficient subscribers could not be found to guarantee the expense” (Wantrup). Note on provenance: the letter was sold in 1985 loosely inserted in a copy of Melville’s Sketches (Kenneth Hince Book Auctions, Melbourne, 29 August 1985, lot 71); subsequently in the collection of Robert Holmes a Court, at which time it appears to have been removed and passed into a Sydney private collection. See Jonathan Wantrup, Thomas and William Boone’s Library of Australian Travels (Melbourne, 2019), p. 11 and illustrated p. 13. Estimate $800/1200 Illustrated online at Invaluable.com

title: MOOR, J.H. NOTICES OF THE INDIAN ARCHIPELAGO, and adjacent countries, being a collection of papers relating to Borneo, C

description: BLAXCELL, Garnham and BENT, Ellis. DISHONOURED PROMISSORY NOTE, manuscript signed by Garnham Blaxcell for 250 pounds to be paid in good Government Bills to Captain Joseph James, Sydney. Together with a printed and manuscript notice of protest form, dated 16 August 1813, signed by Ellis Bent, Judge Advocate, and James Foster, Clerk for Ellis Bent, folio printed form, printed by George Howe, achieved in manuscript by James Foster, the second side being the copy of the original promissory note signed by the debtor, Garnham Blaxcell Manuscript on watermarked paper, 75 x 200 mm, and folio printed form, both pieces with pale staining at right margin. Sydney, March 1812 and [Howe printer] August 1813. A pair of early and important Australian commercial documents. Garnham Blaxcell was one of Sydney’s wealthiest merchants, and together with Alexander Riley and Darcy Wentworth had been granted a monopoly in the importation and sale of rum as part of a contract to build the Sydney Hospital, known thereafter as the “Rum Hospital”. The importation and distribution of rum was a sensitive point following the coup against Governor Bligh, and consequently Bligh’s successor, Governor Lachlan Macquarie, judiciously decided to end the monopoly and allowed rum to be imported and sold in the colony by others. Blaxcell was the worst effected by this reversal and was eventually ruined. By 1812 he was unable to pay import duties to the Government and defaulted on his numerous private debts. On 16 August 1813 an official protest by Joseph James was made to Judge Advocate Ellis Bent, while the Crown was also preparing to recover Blaxcell’s debts through the Supreme Court. Holding on for four more years, Blaxcell left the colony on April 1817 his debts unpaid. He died on the way back to England. This is a significant relic in the early history of New South Wales, encapsulating the corruption of the Rum Corps years and one of the main actors.
